Waller, Opening Remarks
headlines.officialText: The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions. Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings.

Jefferson, Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
headlines.officialText: At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil Thank you, Nigel, for that kind introduction, and thank you to the Central Bank of Brazil and International Monetary Fund for hosting this important conference.1 It is an honor to be here with my fellow panelists. The nature and duration of these shocks influence the approach to monetary policymaking. As a monetary policymaker in the United States, I must consider whether and how shocks impact both sides of our dual mandate—maximum employment and stable prices. When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other.3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff. An energy price shock can push up inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand. The appropriate response depends on the relative costs of missing each objective and the balance of risks. When the recent energy price shock occurred, inflation in the U.S. was already above our 2 percent target. If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted. If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment. Shocks that affect both aggregate supply and aggregated demand but with differential timing are especially challenging for monetary policymakers. Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation. In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth. Labor market effects are relevant as well. economy, my goal is to restore price stability while maintaining a solid labor market. Jefferson, "Navigating Economic Shocks: A Monetary Policymaker's Perspective," speech delivered at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, July 16, 2026. A positive gap signals excess demand, with employment above its maximum sustainable level and upward pressure on inflation; a negative gap signals excess supply, with the opposite effects.

Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee, October 27-28, 2026
headlines.officialText: October 27–28, 2026 A joint meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System was held in the offices of the Board of Governors on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. The staff also highlighted the rapid growth of debt associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, noting that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint. Overall, the staff judged that current vulnerabilities could amplify shocks somewhat more than usual, with elevated asset valuations and leverage at hedge funds representing the most salient vulnerabilities, while strong bank and household balance sheets provided an important buffer against more severe outcomes. In their discussion of financial stability, almost all participants commented on risks associated with a scenario in which the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors. Many participants commented on the potential consequences of an AI-related asset price revaluation should it occur. Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures. A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms. Several participants noted that the staff's assessment was that the financial system remained resilient, with the banking sector well capitalized and able to withstand losses under the severe scenarios considered. However, several participants cautioned that past experience suggested that banking system vulnerabilities could emerge rapidly even after seemingly reassuring initial assessments. Several participants expressed concerns that the existing data available to bank supervisors may not fully capture banks' indirect exposure through nonbank financial institutions, including credit lines to private credit funds and other complex linkages. Most participants highlighted hedge fund leverage or limited dealer intermediation capacity as potential channels of amplification during periods of market stress. Several participants pointed to banks' prime brokerage exposures as warranting continued monitoring and supervisory attention. Some participants raised concerns about potential interactions among the level of government indebtedness, rising long-term yields, and financial stability, noting that the implications of adverse shocks for the economic outlook could be harder to gauge in a situation of diminished fiscal policy space. Some participants also highlighted cyber risk as a critical area of concern. Almost all participants commented on potential policy responses that could address financial stability vulnerabilities. A few participants suggested that maintaining strong bank capital cushions, including through the deployment of the countercyclical capital buffer, would help ensure that commercial banks could continue intermediating credit if stress emerged elsewhere in the financial system. A few participants noted the importance of ensuring ready bank access to the discount window and other liquidity programs. Some participants highlighted potential ways of enhancing operational readiness, including those relating to the Federal Reserve's ability to lend to designated financial market utilities amid stressed conditions, with participants expressing different views on the steps to be taken, if appropriate. A few participants also discussed distinguishing Federal Reserve asset purchases undertaken for market functioning purposes from those undertaken to provide monetary policy accommodation. Several participants stressed that monetary policy was not the appropriate tool to address financial stability risks directly, though a couple of participants noted that monetary policy implementation choices could influence the nonbank sector's incentives to rely on leverage. On net, nominal Treasury yields and inflation compensation were little changed, broad equity prices were marginally higher, and the dollar was stronger. However, asset prices exhibited notable swings over the period, as market participants absorbed economic data releases, financial disclosures by AI companies, evolving developments in the ongoing conflict with Iran, and a sharp repricing of France's sovereign debt. With regard to policy rate expectations, the manager observed that the federal funds rate path implied by futures prices was little changed, on net, over the period, with little chance of a rate increase associated with this meeting but high probabilities assigned to a 25 basis point hike by year-end and two more by the summer of 2027. Expectations derived from the Open Market Desk Survey of Market Expectations (Desk survey) were somewhat lower, with the median participant expecting one rate hike in December and another one in March 2027, followed by a rate cut early in 2028. The Desk survey's median estimate of the longer-run nominal federal funds rate increased to about 3.4 percent; an increase in estimates of the longer-run real interest rate was believed to be the source of this upward shift. The manager assessed that, even before this intermeeting period, the higher interest rate environment was both weighing on equity prices and raising credit spreads. Higher interest rates had helped lower equity valuations and had contributed to greater investor sensitivity regarding more highly leveraged borrowers. Market-implied policy rate paths in major advanced-economy central banks continued to indicate further policy tightening by the end of 2027. policy rate path was little changed on net, market-implied policy rate paths in advanced foreign economies (AFEs) shifted down, in part reflecting perceptions of a less resilient economic outlook than in the U.S. Increased investor concerns over fiscal prospects also weighed on policy rate expectations in the euro area.

headlines.title: Barr, Investing in America’s Underserved Communities
headlines.officialText: So I will start with the economic outlook. Overall, the economy is strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment. But inflation is too high, making it hard for American families to make ends meet. And that's why it is so important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to our target of 2 percent in a timely way. Of course, I'll continue to monitor the incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks in making that assessment. And while economic activity and employment are continuing to grow for the country as a whole, not all families and communities are thriving. Community organizations and national nonprofits can reduce the costs of acquiring and interpreting information about low-income borrowers and communities, they can coordinate lending to overcome collective action problems, and they can also share risks to reduce bank exposures. Not far from here, in a part of Brooklyn marked by limited housing as well as a lack of employment and healthy food sources, private and public partners came together in a project called City Point, which includes a full-service supermarket, 120 affordable housing units, and retail space for local small businesses. I've seen what public–private partnerships mean for employment and small business growth in Cleveland, Ohio, and I've seen a business incubator in Atlanta, Georgia, make a real difference to its local community. In one part of this building, staff are working every day to help implement monetary policy, help ensure smooth financial markets, and promote a strong economy.
